extracted.intended_audience: aspiring authors and historians (young aspirants to authorship; writers preparing a history for publication)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and standards for authorship in general and for composing a multi-volume history: research practices, composition workflow, dealings with publishers, revision and proofreading, and expectations about readership and errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condense news to the gist for the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Give in fewer words the gist of the information, in so far, at least, as it would be likely to interest our rural readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice condensing and selecting material that is relevant to your intended readership; editorial apprenticeship (condensing city foreign news for a rural paper) teaches this skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apprenticeship and gradual improvement via newspaper work
rubrics_metrics.description: Acquire rudimentary knowledge of composition by working in newspaper offices: selection, condensation, and preparing matter for print.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long experience as a journeyman or printer of various newspapers gradually improves skills; early, practical editorial work is valuable preparation for authorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the appropriate literary form (prose vs. verse)
rubrics_metrics.description: If poetic expression is defective, renounce verse and utter thoughts in unmistakable prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be honest about your strengths; prefer the form that best suits your ability to express ideas clearly rather than forcing an ill-suited form (e.g., verse when not gifted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand publishers' economic requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: No judicious publisher will buy a manuscript from an unknown author unless there is reason to expect a public for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that most first works do not pay publication costs; publishers avoid financial risk. Authors often need a pre-existing audience or take on publication costs themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a public/audience before expecting a publisher
rubrics_metrics.description: Each author had great need of a public; a publisher rarely risks on an unknown author because the great mass of readers follow established fame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate readership (e.g., newspaper columns, letters) before seeking a book publisher; marketability is crucial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect copious primary materials and authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect such materials as were then accessible: documents, official reports, newspaper letters, etc.; consult public libraries and historical societies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple archives and libraries (Society, Historical, Astor, Mercantile) and search out contemporary sources to build the substance of chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read, compare, and digest sources before composing
rubrics_metrics.description: When I had the substance of my next chapter pretty fairly in mind, I began to compose that chapter; having often several authorities conveniently disposed around me.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare and arrange materials thoroughly before drafting; digestion of sources leads to better-organized chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a dedicated workspace and minimize interruptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Our rule was to lock the door on resuming composition, and decline all solicitations to open it till the day's allotted task had been finished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish a 'den' or workshop, restrict access to one trusted person plus your secretary, and guard working hours to maintain focus and productivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ assistants (secretary) and use dictation/transcription
rubrics_metrics.description: I oftener wrote out my first draft, merely indicating extracts; but I sometimes dictated to my secretary, who took short-hand notes and wrote them out at his leisure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a secretary for transcription and insertion of quoted extracts; dictation and shorthand can accelerate composition when managed properly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compose deliberately: allow days per chapter and iterate drafts
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually, two days, or even three, were given to the composition of each of the longer chapters, after I had prepared and digested its material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set realistic timeblocks for chapters based on length and complexity; expect multiple drafts and time for digestion of material before finalizing a chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous proofreading and staged corrections with the stereotyper
rubrics_metrics.description: A chapter having been fairly written out or transcribed, I carefully revised and sent it to the stereotyper, who sent me his second and third proofs, which were successively corrected before the pages were ready to be cast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple proof stages (first, second, third proofs) and correct each; engage with the stereotyper/printer to catch and fix errors before casting pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be ready to revise or recast chapters when new material appears
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes, the discovery of new material compelled the revision and recast of a chapter which had been passed as complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain flexibility: new documents or reports can necessitate substantive rewrites even after a chapter was considered finished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect imperfect and contradictory sources; practice source criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: The material was very copious ... it was still exceedingly imperfect and contradictory. I found reports conflicting (e.g., officers reported killed who later fought).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check authorities, be skeptical of single reports, and be prepared to correct errors discovered post-publication; recognize the limits of available records, especially for recent events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off: more particulars increases chance of factual errors but value to historians
rubrics_metrics.description: As I have stated many more particulars than my rivals ... it is probable that my work originally embodied more errors of fact or incident than almost any other. Yet 'The American Conflict' will be consulted, at least by historians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the benefit of thoroughness against the higher risk of including inadvertent factual mistakes; detailed works may be more useful to future scholars despite early errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage personal expectations about fame and profit
rubrics_metrics.description: Green authors are apt to suffer from disappointment ... Not one first work in a hundred ever pays the cost of its publication. True, yours may be the rare exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate modest financial returns and limited immediate recognition for initial works; pursue authorship for vocation and contribution rather than guaranteed fortune.
